scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the Asshole)** Here's why, broken down ethically and emotionally: ### ️ **You did the right thing by telling your sister** - Cheating is a breach of trust, and **your sister had a right to know**. You didn't cover it up or protect G— you prioritized her autonomy. That's *not* AITA; it's responsible and mature. - If you * hadn't* told her, * that* would have been the real betrayal (to her and to your own integrity). ### ️ **Forgiving G doesn't mean you condone his actions** - You explicitly said: "I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it." That's healthy. Forgiveness isn't about excusing the behavior—it's about *your* ability to move forward without being consumed by anger. - G's genuine remorse ( crying, which he rarely does) matters. People can change, and 13 years of friendship isn't something to discard over one mistake *if* the person is truly sorry and has taken responsibility. ### ️ **Your loyalty to your sister ≠ your loyalty to your best friend** - **This is the critical point:** Your sister is *not* entitled to dictate who you can be friends with. - She's hurt, so her anger is understandable—but her expectation that you "choose" her over your best friend is **unreasonable**. - You're not " taking sides" by remaining friends with G. You're simply **maintaining your own relationship** with him, separate from her relationship with him. - * "Would I end a friendship if my best friend cheated on their SO? No."* **This is 100% correct logic.** The fact that the SO is your sister doesn't change the principle. - **Family dynamics don't override personal bonds:** You don't "owe" your sister a permanent estrangement from your best friend. Her hurt is real, but it's *hers* to process—not yours to fix by cutting off a 13-year friendship. ### ️ **Practical reality matters** - You're going to different colleges. This isn't a " daily tension" situation. - You're not enabling G or helping him hide anything. He's already broken up with your sister, and you're not involved in their dynamic anymore. - **" making me feel like shit for still being friends with G"** is emotional manipulation. *You* get to decide who stays in your life based on *your* values, not her guilt trips. ### 💡 **What * would* be AITA?** - If you * hadn't* told your sister about the affair. - If you were actively helping G manipulate or contact her against her wishes. - If you were gaslighting her (" it's not a big deal, just get over it") instead of acknowledging her pain while also protecting your own boundaries. - **None of those apply here.** ### 🌟 **Final thought:** You're not the asshole—you're a person trying to navigate a painful situation with **integrity**. You told the truth, you're holding G accountable ( by not " 100% getting over it"), and you're setting boundaries * for yourself* ( by not cutting ties over one mistake). Your sister's anger is her own to work through, but ** she doesn get to dictate your friendships**. - **Do this:** Tell her: " I love you, and I'm sorry you're hurt. But G and I have been best friends for 13 years. I'm not going to end that over this. I hope you can respect that, even if you don't agree." - **Then** focus on your own healing. You did the right thing. Period. - **P.S.** If her pressure continues, it's okay to distance yourself * from her* for a while. You can't be her emotional enforcer while also being true to yourself. **You're not the problem here.** 💪

Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is an 18-year-old guy asking if he's the asshole for maintaining friendship with his best friend G after G cheated on his twin sister. 

First, I need to consider the dynamics here. They've been friends since kindergarten, so 13 years of history. G and his sister had a " thing" for years before dating, then broke up after the affair. The user feels torn between loyalty to his sister and his lifelong friendship with G. 

Hmm... the key points are:
- He told his sister about the affair (which was the right thing to do)
- He forgave G after G's genuine remorse (G cried, which he rarely does)
- His sister is upset he's still friends with G
- They're going to different colleges soon, so physical proximity won't be an issue
- His reasoning: "Would I end a friendship if my best friend cheated on their SO? No, so why different because it's my sister?"

*Pausing to analyze the ethical layers...*

The core tension here is between two valid loyalties: family vs. friendship. But "AITA" framing assumes one side is "wrong," which oversimplifies it. 

*Checking societal norms:*
- Cheating is objectively wrong, no dispute there
- But ending a 13-year friendship over one infidelity? That's... extreme. Most people wouldn't cut ties permanently over a single mistake, especially with someone who's genuinely remorseful. 
- The fact that he told his sister immediately shows he didn't cover it up - that's crucial. He didn't protect G; he prioritized his sister's right to know.

*What's the sister's perspective?*
- She's hurt, so naturally she wants G cut out of her life. 
- But her anger at her brother for not " taking sides" is... problematic. He's not her enforcer; he's her brother with his own relationships. 
- " making me feel like shit for still being friends with G" - that's emotional manipulation. He doesn't owe her that.

*His reasoning about " would I end a friendship if it wasn't my sister?"* is actually spot-on. The relationship dynamic shouldn't change the principle. If G had cheated on a random girlfriend, he'd still be friends with G (assuming G's remorse was genuine). The only difference is the added layer of family, but that doesn't make his friendship less valid.

* potential red flags:*
- Is he enabling G? (But he's not "enabling" - he's not helping G hide anything, and G's already broken up with his sister)
- Is he being disloyal to his sister? (No - he told her the truth, which is the only ethical choice. His continued friendship with G doesn't mean he's condoning the cheating)

*Final judgment:*
- He's not the asshole. 
- His sister's expectations are unreasonable. 
- He's balancing two painful loyalties healthily: he didn't cover up the affair (sister's right), but he's not severing a 13-year bond over one mistake (his own right). 
- The " different colleges" point is relevant - they'll be physically separated, so no ongoing tension. 

*Why " not AITA"?* 
- He did the right thing by telling his sister immediately 
- Forgiveness doesn't equal condoning 
- His friendship with G is separate from his sister's relationship with G 
- He's not being disloyal to his sister by maintaining his own friendship 

...Though I should note: if G continues to be unrepentant or manipulative, that's different. But based on what he described (G crying, genuinely sorry), it's reasonable to maintain the friendship while still being clear about boundaries.
